parsed.explanation: Thin-data territory criminalising same-sex conduct under both frameworks (six months to three years), with no protections documented and courts of the administering state shown to operate on dubious political charges from the territory. No trans-specific statute, no documented trans visitor case, and no documented universal-exposure measure — so the worst documented feature is tier-3 (societal hostility with thin recourse) plus a live criminal statute whose trans application is an open question. Per rule 13 the structural signals — criminalisation, no relief, no protective infrastructure, social climate reading same-sex relations as a foreign phenomenon — resolve below the midpoint, but above the 0.35 anchors because no visitor-facing register, sweep, or routine targeting is documented.

entry_documents.exposure: Document/marker rules for the territory are not addressed by any source; a visitor's exposure at entry is not documented.
entry_documents.interaction: Administering state controls most ground and its entry processes; which framework applies depends on location.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Administering state's courts and detention operate on the territory's cases; 2005 trial of seven defenders on dubious charges documents court/detention reach. Camp officials held prisoners on 'homosexuality' charges (2009), allegedly on facts describing rape.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: Criminalisation operative under both frameworks; camp administration exercises charge power outside courts.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: Facilities access, ward placement, and facilities rules for trans visitors are not addressed by any source.

care_services.exposure: Trans-specific medical care and HRT access are not addressed by any source for this territory.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: Same-sex intimacy criminalised under both frameworks (six months–three years; up to three years in the movement's self-proclaimed state, per 2017 monitors). Same-sex relations widely read as a foreign phenomenon in a Muslim-majority society.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: 2010 diplomatic statement describes constitutional silence — a position, not decriminalisation; no statute decriminalises.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Statute application to trans people, and legal-sex reading, is unsourced.

minors_guardians.exposure: No source addresses minors travelling with a trans adult; the same criminalisation regime applies to any accompanying adult whose relationship is read as same-sex under birth-sex status.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: Refugee-aid organisation: no protection for LGBTQ individuals against discrimination or violence — recourse gap documented.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Police response to anti-trans violence is unsourced; the recourse gap implies hostility would go unremedied.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: Open questions: whether either authority applies same-sex provisions to trans people, document rules, facilities, custody placement, care access.
remedies_unknowns.protection: None documented anywhere in the inventory.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Administering state courts reachable but shown hearing dubious political charges; camp charges bypass courts entirely.

anchor_checks.comparison: 0.35-A rests on a universal, routine border register excluding trans visitors. This dossier documents no visitor-facing universal-exposure measure; only a criminal statute with unsourced trans application and an unremedied social-recourse gap. That places this case above 0.35-A.

0.55-B features administrative border screening with written decisions and appeal desks — remedies that exist even if slow. Here no remedy is documented at all for LGBTQ people, and criminal penalties (up to three years) exceed 0.55-B's administrative refusal. This case sits below 0.55-B.

0.75-C documents trained border officers, a functioning tribunal, compensation for unlawful detention, and release as the typical outcome. This territory documents dubious political trials, camp charges outside courts, and zero documented recourse. It is materially below 0.75-C.

0.15-C documents morality sweeps with decoy encounters, coerced statements, and custodial violence as a pattern. No such organised targeting of gender-nonconforming or trans visitors is documented here; enforcement is recorded only in camps and listings, so the case stays above 0.15.

parsed.synthesis: The combined operative regime is two criminalising frameworks over one ground: the administering state's courts and detention demonstrably reach the territory (dubious 2005 political trial), while the movement's camp administration holds prisoners on homosexuality charges outside any court. No protective machinery, remedy, or trans-specific processing is documented anywhere; the sole positive (a diplomat's constitutional-silence claim) is explicitly not decriminalisation. Social climate reads same-sex relations as foreign, with a documented no-recourse finding for LGBTQ victims. Under the thin-data rule the structural facts — dual criminalisation, no relief, no protection, fragile courts — resolve the score below the midpoint, while the complete absence of any documented trans-visitor exposure or universal-exposure measure keeps it out of the 0.35 band. Uncertainty is substantial but cuts against safety, not toward it.
